prompt: Which command prints the compiler's escape analysis decisions for the package in `./point`?
hint: The flags go to the compiler, not the linker.

choices.text: `go vet -m ./point`
choices.why: `go vet` runs static checks over the source; it has no `-m` and does not report where values are allocated.

choices.text: `go build -gcflags=-m ./point`
choices.why: Right. `-gcflags` passes `-m` to `go tool compile`, whose help calls it "print optimization decisions", escape analysis among them.

choices.text: `go build -ldflags=-m ./point`
choices.why: `-ldflags` goes to the linker, which runs after every allocation decision has been made, and only for a program.

choices.text: `go test -benchmem ./point`
choices.why: `-benchmem` counts allocations a benchmark made at run time; it says nothing about the compiler's reasons.

prompt: Match each line of `-gcflags=-m` output with what it says.
hint: One description is not something `-m` ever reports.

pairs.right: the named variable p is allocated on the heap
the function keeps nothing this parameter points at
what a points at may come back out as the result
the function is small enough to be copied into callers

right_distractors: the value was freed by the garbage collector

prompt: `Farther(a, b *Point) *Point` is reported as `leaking param: a to result ~r0 level=0`. A caller writes `q := Point{3, 4}` and `n := Sum(Farther(&q, &q))`, keeping no pointer afterwards. Where can `q` live?
hint: "Leaking param" is a summary the caller reads, not an allocation.

choices.text: On the heap, because any parameter that leaks moves its argument there
choices.why: That is the plain `leaking param: c` form. "To result" sends the decision back to the caller.

choices.text: On the stack, because `Sum` keeps nothing it is given
choices.why: Right. The pointer comes back out of `Farther` and goes into `Sum`, whose `p does not escape`, so nothing outlives the caller.

choices.text: Inside `Farther`'s frame, copied there when it is called
choices.why: Passing a pointer copies the pointer, not the `Point`; `Farther` has no copy of `q`.

choices.text: Nowhere until the collector decides, at run time
choices.why: Where a value lives is decided once, at compile time; the collector only frees what is already on the heap.

prompt: In a module `example.com/shop`, `go build -gcflags=-m .` on the `main` package prints dozens of lines, none about `internal/cart`, which `main` imports and which you know returns pointers. What explains it?
hint: Which packages does `-gcflags` reach without a pattern?

choices.text: The build cache had `internal/cart` already, so it was not compiled again
choices.why: The cache is not the reason here: without a pattern the flags never applied to `cart` at all, cached or not.

choices.text: Returned pointers only show up with `-m=2`
choices.why: `-m` already prints `moved to heap` and `escapes to heap`; `-m=2` adds the reasons.

choices.text: Without a pattern the flags reach only `main`
choices.why: Right. Without a pattern the list applies to the packages named on the command line, here `main` alone; `-gcflags='example.com/shop/...=-m'` reaches `cart`.

choices.text: An `internal` package is hidden from the compiler's report
choices.why: `internal` limits who may import a package; `hits`'s `internal/tally` was reported as soon as a pattern named it.

prompt: `func Show(n int) { fmt.Println(n) }` is reported as `n escapes to heap`. Why does a plain `int` escape?
hint: What is `Println`'s parameter type, and what does `-m=2` say about `Fprintln`?

choices.text: `Println` takes `...any`, and `Fprintln`'s parameter leaks to the heap
choices.why: Right. An interface points at its data, and the summary for `Fprintln` says its arguments leak, so `n` gets a heap copy.

choices.text: Every integer argument to a function is passed on the heap
choices.why: `Sum(p)` and countless other calls pass integers in registers or on the stack; this one escapes because of the interface.

choices.text: `Println` is inlined, and inlined code always allocates
choices.why: Inlining usually removes allocations, as `Distance` showed; here the leak is in `Fprintln`, which was not inlined.

choices.text: The slice of arguments escapes, taking `n` with it
choices.why: The report says `... argument does not escape`: the slice stays on the stack and only the value put into it moves.

prompt: `Counter` declares `n := 0` and returns `func() int { n++; return n }`. The report says `moved to heap: n`. Why could `n` not stay in `Counter`'s frame?
hint: When does the closure run?

choices.text: Closures are always allocated on the heap, whatever they capture
choices.why: `Total`'s closure, passed to `Each`, did not escape: `func literal does not escape` under `-l`.

choices.text: It is still changed by a closure running after the call has ended
choices.why: Right. The closure is returned and keeps a reference to `n`, and it increments `n` when the frame is already gone.

choices.text: `n` is an `int`, and an `int` captured by reference is boxed like an interface
choices.why: No interface is involved; the reason is lifetime, and a captured `*Point` would move for the same reason.

choices.text: `n++` writes to `n`, and the stack is read-only after a function starts
choices.why: A frame is ordinary writable memory; `t += x` in `Total` writes a captured variable on the stack.

prompt: Which of these make the value named escape to the heap? Choose every one that does.
hint: Ask, for each, whether anything can reach the value after the function returns.

choices.text: A function returns `c.Tick`, a method value on its parameter `c`
choices.why: Yes. `Ticker` showed it: `c.Tick escapes to heap` and `leaking param: c`.

choices.text: A function stores `string(b)` as a key with `m[string(b)]++`
choices.why: Yes. A map keeps its keys, and `Add` was reported `string(b) escapes to heap`.

choices.text: A function only reads `m[string(b)]`
choices.why: A lookup keeps nothing: `Get` was reported `string(b) does not escape`.

choices.text: A function passes `&x` to `Sum`, whose `p does not escape`
choices.why: That summary is exactly what lets `x` stay in the caller's frame.

choices.text: A function uses `f := c.Tick` and calls `f()` twice
choices.why: Used locally, the method value stays on the stack: `c.Tick does not escape` in `TickTwice`.

prompt: A package keeps `var handlers []*Handler` and has `func Register(h *Handler) { handlers = append(handlers, h) }`. What does `-m` report for `h`, and what follows for a caller that writes `Register(&Handler{})`?
hint: Where does `h` end up: in a result, or somewhere that outlives every call?

choices.text: `h does not escape`, since `append` copies the pointer
choices.why: Copying the pointer into a slice that is kept is exactly how what it points at gets kept.

choices.text: `leaking param: h to result ~r0 level=0`, so the caller decides
choices.why: `Register` has no result; `h` goes into a package-level slice, which is the heap.

choices.text: `append escapes to heap`, which affects only the slice, not the `Handler`
choices.why: The growing array does escape, but so does every `Handler` stored in it.

choices.text: `leaking param: h`, so the caller's `&Handler{}` escapes to the heap
choices.why: Right. A parameter stored in a global leaks to the heap itself, and every argument passed to it moves there, as `Ticker(&clk)` moved `clk`.

prompt: `Sized(n)` does `s := make([]int, n)` and is reported `make([]int, n) does not escape`, yet `testing.AllocsPerRun` counts one allocation for `Sized(5)`. How can both be true?
hint: What does the compiler put in the frame when it cannot know `n`?

choices.text: The report is wrong for `make`, and newer releases fix it
choices.why: The report answers a different question, lifetime, and answers it correctly: the slice does not outlive `Sized`.

choices.text: Only 32 bytes are reserved in the frame
choices.why: Right. A check is compiled in, and the heap is used when the slice does not fit them. Four `int`s fit in 32 bytes and five do not, so `Sized(4)` costs nothing and `Sized(5)` one allocation.

choices.text: `AllocsPerRun` counts the test's closure, not `Sized`
choices.why: `Sized(4)`, called through the same kind of closure, counted 0.

choices.text: Five is over the 64 KiB limit for an implicit value
choices.why: Five `int`s are 40 bytes; the 64 KiB limit is what sent `make([]int, 10000)` to the heap.

prompt: With the 32-byte buffer Go 1.27 reserves for a `make` whose length is only known at run time, what is the largest `n` for which `make([]string, n)` stays on the stack on linux/amd64, where a string header is 16 bytes?
hint: Divide the buffer by the element size and round down.

prompt: After `//go:noinline` is put above `point.New`, the report for `why/inline.go` loses `inlining call to point.New` and `&point.Point{...} does not escape`. Nothing in `Distance` changed. What happened to the `Point`?
hint: Whose frame is the `Point` made in once `New` is a real call?

choices.text: It still lives in `Distance`'s frame; only the message disappeared
choices.why: `AllocsPerRun` counted `Distance(4, 5)` going from 0 to 1 allocation with the directive on.

choices.text: It is made inside `New` and returned, so it is on the heap
choices.why: Right. Inlined, the `&Point{...}` was `Distance`'s own value; called, it is `New`'s, and `New` returns its address.

choices.text: The directive forbids allocation, so `New` now fails to build
choices.why: `//go:noinline` only stops the inliner; the build succeeded and `New`'s own verdict was unchanged.

choices.text: `Sum` stops being inlined too, which moves the `Point`
choices.why: The report still says `inlining call to point.Sum`; the change is in `New` alone.

prompt: To see what each function decides on its own, with no callee copied into it, Ana builds with `go build -gcflags='-m ___' ./why`, the compiler flag that turns inlining off.
hint: A single lower-case letter after a dash.

prompt: The report says `n escapes to heap` for `func Box(n int) any { return n }`, yet `testing.AllocsPerRun` counts 0 for `Box(7)` and 1 for `Box(1000)`. Why the difference?
hint: Look in `runtime/iface.go` for a table.

choices.text: Small constants are folded at compile time, so `Box(7)` is never called
choices.why: The test passes the values through package-level variables precisely so that nothing is known in advance.

choices.text: Values from 0 to 255 point into a table the runtime keeps
choices.why: Right. `staticuint64s` holds them, so the interface points there instead of at a new copy.

choices.text: `AllocsPerRun` rounds averages below one down to zero
choices.why: It returns the average as a float; `Box(1000)` was exactly 1 and `Box(7)` exactly 0.

choices.text: An `int` under 256 fits in the interface's type word
choices.why: The type word holds the type; the value is reached through the data pointer either way.

prompt: With `//go:noinline` on `point.New`, `BenchmarkDistance` took 17.03 ns/op with 1 alloc/op, while `BenchmarkCall`, the same work behind a non-inlined call with no allocation, took 0.7961 ns/op. About how many nanoseconds of `Distance`'s time are the allocation rather than the call?
hint: Subtract the call's time.

prompt: A colleague concludes from the benchmark that a heap allocation costs exactly 16 ns and that a hot path with one million of them costs 16 ms in total. What does that leave out?
hint: Who frees the memory, and on which processor?

choices.text: Nothing: `-benchmem` already includes the collector's time
choices.why: It counts bytes and allocations; ns/op holds only the share of collection that landed on the benchmark's goroutine.

choices.text: The stack, which is also freed by the collector
choices.why: A frame is freed by returning from the function; the collector has no stack work to do for it.

choices.text: The collector's work later, part of it on other processors
choices.why: Right. Each object has to be found and freed afterwards, and that work is mostly outside the ns/op of the loop that allocated it.

choices.text: Only the 0.8 ns of the call, which should be subtracted
choices.why: That makes the estimate smaller still; the missing cost goes the other way.

prompt: In `hits`, `Count`'s `string(bufio.s.token)` escapes because `Parse`'s `line` leaks through `strings.Fields(line)`, the fallback that ran on none of the 100,000 lines. Why does a path that never runs decide it?
hint: When is escape analysis done?

choices.text: The fallback runs once at start-up to warm the cache
choices.why: Nothing like that happens; `split5` accepted every line `genlog` wrote.

choices.text: At compile time, over every path in the code
choices.why: Right. No input exists yet when the decision is made, so one path that leaks is enough for every caller.

choices.text: Profile-guided optimisation marked the fallback as hot
choices.why: No profile was given to the compiler, and a profile would show the fallback as never taken.

choices.text: `strings.Fields` was inlined, and inlined calls count twice
choices.why: Nothing counts twice; the leak comes from `Fields`'s summary for its parameter.

prompt: Put in order the steps of the route `-m=2` reported last for the string of each line in `hits`, once both `Clone`s were in place, from where the string is made to where it has to outlive the loop.
hint: It ends in the line labelled `key of map put`.
items: `Count` converts the scanner's bytes to a string on line 64
the string is passed to `Parse` as `line`
`Parse` returns `Path` as a piece of `line` inside the `Entry`
`Count` stores `e.Path` as a key in `s.ByPath` on line 70

prompt: Somebody keeps both `strings.Clone` edits in `tally.go`, so that `Parse` reports `leaking param: line to result ~r0 level=0`, and expects `Count` over 100,000 lines to drop from 100,009 allocations to about 9. What happens?
hint: Two more things stand between the line and the stack.

choices.text: It drops to 9, since nothing in `Parse` leaks to the heap
choices.why: `Count` itself still stores `e.Path` as a map key, and the report says the string escapes for that reason.

choices.text: It rises, since each `Clone` allocates on every line
choices.why: The fallback's `Clone` runs on no line of `genlog`'s log, though the one before `ParseDuration` would run on every line.

choices.text: It stays at one per line
choices.why: Right. The map key is the third route, and even with no route a line of 34 to 51 bytes is longer than the 32-byte stack buffer a string conversion gets. The `Clone` before `ParseDuration` even adds one.

choices.text: It drops to half, since one of the three routes is still open
choices.why: Routes are not shares of an allocation: any single one is enough to put the whole string on the heap.

prompt: `TestAllocs` reported `Parse` at 0 allocations, `Count` over 1,000 lines at 1009 and over 100,000 lines at 100009. What do the three numbers say together?
hint: Compare the two counts of `Count` with their line counts.

choices.text: `Parse` allocates once per line and `Count` adds nine
choices.why: `Parse` was measured alone at 0; the allocation per line happens in `Count`, in the string `Text` makes.

choices.text: `Count` allocates nine times per line, rounded
choices.why: Nine per line would be 9,000 and 900,000; the numbers are lines plus nine.

choices.text: One allocation per line in `Count`, plus nine per call
choices.why: Right. 1,009 − 1,000 and 100,009 − 100,000 are both 9: a fixed cost per count, the two maps among it, and one string per line.

choices.text: The allocations grow faster than the input, so something leaks
choices.why: They grow exactly with the input, one per line; a leak would show as a growing difference.

prompt: Which of these tells you how many heap allocations a function actually makes when it runs?
hint: One of them runs the code; the others read it.

choices.text: `go build -gcflags=-m=2`
choices.why: It prints the compiler's predictions and their reasons; `Box(7)` escaped in it and allocated nothing.

choices.text: `testing.AllocsPerRun`
choices.why: Right. It runs the function and counts, which is how `Sized(5)` was caught allocating with `does not escape`.

choices.text: `go vet`
choices.why: `go vet` reports suspicious code and runs nothing.

choices.text: `go build -gcflags=all=-m`
choices.why: It is the same prediction for every package in the build, 44,067 lines for `hits`.

prompt: Lesson 13's `split5` returns `[5]string`; `strings.Fields` returns `[]string`. Both point into the same line. Why does one cost an allocation per call and the other none?
hint: Where does each result's storage live, and is its size known when compiling?

choices.text: Arrays are always on the stack and slices always on the heap
choices.why: `make([]int, 64)` in `Fixed` stayed on the stack, and `Grid`'s 1 MiB array went to the heap.

choices.text: `strings.Fields` copies every field, and the copies are what allocate
choices.why: Both return strings that point into the line without copying it; the difference is the container holding them.

choices.text: The array is copied out by value
choices.why: Right. A fixed-size array is copied into the caller's frame, and `split5`'s report is `leaking param: line to result f`. `Fields` returns a slice whose array it made, of a size known only at run time, so that array outlives the call on the heap.

choices.text: `split5` is inlined into `Parse`, which removes its allocation
choices.why: The report for `tally` printed no `inlining call to split5`; the array is free because it is returned by value.

prompt: A request handler shows `id escapes to heap` for `log.Printf("request %d", id)`. Before rewriting the logging, what is the first thing worth doing?
hint: The report is a prediction; what turns it into a decision?

choices.text: Rewrite the call at once, since every escape is a performance bug
choices.why: Many escapes are necessary or cheap, like the maps `Count` returns; rewriting without a measurement trades clarity for nothing known.

choices.text: Build with `-l` to see whether the escape survives without inlining
choices.why: `-l` builds a binary nobody ships; the verdict that matters is the one with inlining on.

choices.text: Measure first: count its allocations and see whether this path is hot
choices.why: Right. Count them, and look in a profile. An `id` below 256 allocates nothing at all, and a path that runs once a request is one small cost among everything else the request does.

choices.text: Switch `id` to a pointer, so that the interface holds a pointer it already has
choices.why: A pointer to `id` would make `id` itself escape, and the call would still allocate.
